rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window, identify critical pairs, and minimize the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Make the gradient one step shallower to test whether the critical pair responds to slope. The modest extension should keep the last peak near or below 10 minutes while preserving the other separations.

The critical pair improves with a shallower gradient. Narrowing the solvent window further reduces the slope, while the higher starting organic fraction should offset much of the added retention and keep the last peak near 10 minutes.

Narrow the gradient window another step to bring the critical pair above R = 1.5. Raising the starting organic fraction should compensate for the shallower slope sufficiently to keep the last peak below 10 minutes, with ample separation remaining between the early peaks.

The maximum CRF is already achieved, so test a modest temperature increase to shorten the fully resolved run. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates temperature’s effect on the critical pair, whose resolution margin is small.

Test whether a larger temperature shift carries the critical pair through an elution-order reversal and restores separation while shortening retention. Keep the gradient fixed to isolate temperature effects, retaining injection 4 as the maximum-score fallback.

Shorten the gradient by one step to test whether the new critical pair separates better at a steeper slope. This also probes a faster route to full resolution, while injection 4 remains the maximum-score fallback.

Test a faster high-temperature regime: the observed temperature and slope trends suggest the current critical pair may reverse order and regain separation. This is an exploratory shortcut toward a shorter fully resolved run; injection 4 already secures the maximum CRF.

Test one step shorter at 60 C to see whether the apparently reordered critical pair gains separation with a steeper gradient. Monitor the neighboring pair, currently at R = 2.12, for loss of resolution as the run compresses.

Explore the cooler-temperature branch, since heating initially collapsed the critical separation at 40 C. A shorter gradient tests whether improved temperature selectivity can support full resolution in less time, while the lower starting organic fraction protects early-peak retention.

Shift the fast 60 C gradient upward while preserving its slope to test starting-solvent selectivity around the unresolved middle pair. This should shorten retention further, but early-pair resolution will need close monitoring.

Refine the nearly fully resolved 55 C method by lowering the starting organic fraction to improve separation of the new critical middle pair. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, offering a potential maximum-score method faster than injection 4.

Shorten injection 12 by one gradient-time step to seek a faster maximum-score method. The middle pair at R = 2.20 has room to compress, while prior 55 C runs suggest the tighter pair may maintain or slightly improve its resolution as the gradient steepens.

Trim the unused high-organic end of injection 13 and shorten the programmed gradient, increasing its slope only slightly. This should reduce the last-peak time while keeping both critical pairs near or above R = 1.5.

Lower the starting organic fraction to improve the slope-sensitive middle separation, while steepening the gradient to offset the added retention. This tests whether full resolution can be retained in a slightly shorter run than injection 14.

With several maximum-score methods secured, explore the low-temperature selectivity regime for a faster alternative. The shorter gradient limits retention time while testing whether further cooling separates the congested cluster seen at 35 C through changes in elution order.

Return to the fastest fully resolved method, injection 15, and increase the endpoint by one step to test a slightly steeper gradient. This probes the speed limit directly; if the middle pair falls below R = 1.5, retain injection 15 as the faster fully resolved fallback.

Test a faster version of the original maximum-score method by shifting its starting organic fraction upward while preserving the gradient slope. This isolates the starting-solvent effect and checks whether the critical separation survives the reduction in retention time.

Test a slightly shallower version of injection 6 to lift its R = 1.41 pair above baseline resolution while retaining the stronger separation of the other critical pair. This targets a maximum-score method with more resolution margin than injection 15 and a last peak still below 10 minutes.

With the maximum CRF secured, test the unexplored 50 C regime using a short gradient for a potentially faster separation. The lower starting organic fraction protects the early pair, while this run checks whether temperature and slope together can separate the middle cluster.

Refine the successful 55 C region with a slightly shallower slope than injection 14 to improve its limiting middle separation. This targets full resolution with a little more margin while keeping the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

Trim injection 15’s unused gradient tail while preserving its successful slope and temperature. The last peak previously eluted near organic fraction 0.57, so this endpoint should preserve full resolution and the 7.60-minute last-peak time with a shorter programmed gradient.

Trim injection 13’s unused gradient tail while preserving its slope, which delivered full resolution with slightly more margin than the fastest method. The last peak should still elute inside the gradient near 8 minutes, retaining the maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient.

Test a small slope increase beyond injection 14 to locate the faster boundary of full resolution at this starting composition. The limiting pair may fall just below R = 1.5; injection 22 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-score method.

Use the final injection to refine the fully resolved region between injections 6 and 19, targeting both critical pairs above R = 1.5 with the last peak below 10 minutes. Injection 22 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-score method; this candidate seeks a larger resolution margin.
